blackbeard-hypersonic-missile-ground-lau.content:
Castelion, the defense startup developing the Pentagon's low-cost hypersonic missile, has released what appears to be the first image of its Blackbeard weapon being fired from a ground launcher, offering a new look at the containerized launch architecture the U.S. Army is pursuing.

The photograph, posted by the company on X, shows a Blackbeard missile leaving a launcher mounted on a high-mobility truck chassis — apparently the converted Oshkosh MKR18 truck the company has used in earlier testing. While Blackbeard test vehicles are now a familiar sight, the image is the first public glimpse of how Castelion intends to package and operate the ground-launched version of the weapon, known as Blackbeard GL.

## An affordable hypersonic for the Army

The Army's interest in Blackbeard is rooted in cost as much as performance. The service wants an affordable, mass-produced hypersonic precision-fire capability for time-sensitive, moving, and hardened targets — with a stated objective of roughly 80 percent of the planned Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) Increment 4's capability at a substantially lower cost per round.

The concept is to treat a hypersonic weapon more like a conventional tactical munition than a strategic asset. Existing U.S. hypersonic systems such as the Army's Dark Eagle Long Range Hypersonic Weapon rely on large, highly specialized launch equipment. Blackbeard is instead being built around a containerized launcher compatible with the existing Multiple Launch Rocket System Family of Munitions (MFOM) ecosystem — and eventually the M142 HIMARS fire-control system — so the Army can add a hypersonic effect without a separate launcher, crew, transport, and reload architecture.

The Army's plan calls for an initial ground-launch demonstration using a modified MFOM pod, followed by Blackbeard GL prototypes and a dedicated launcher pod, culminating in a minimum-viable-product flight test using HIMARS fire control. The Army's Fiscal Year 2027 budget documents list a live-fire launch of a "production representative" Blackbeard GL and launcher pod among the program's milestones.

## What is known — and what is not

Castelion unveiled the weapon's current external configuration earlier this year: a two-stage arrangement with a booster and an upper vehicle consistent with a hypersonic glide or maneuvering payload. The ground-launch model lacks the cruciform tailfins seen on the air-launched version. The precise propulsion system and flight profile remain undisclosed, and little is known about its performance parameters.

The company has hinted the missile could strike targets just under 500 miles away, though ground launch — without an aircraft's altitude and speed — would likely shorten that. The pictured launcher uses a compact enclosed container; The War Zone estimates at least two and perhaps as many as four missiles would fit a single launcher. Castelion has stressed that its test hardware is deliberately designed for rapid development cycles and should not necessarily be taken as representative of the final weapon.

It is also worth noting what remains unproven: analysts have pointed out that it is not yet certain whether Blackbeard is a true hypersonic glide vehicle or something closer to a maneuvering ballistic missile — a distinction the company has not fully resolved publicly.

## A Pentagon bet on mass production

Behind the program sits an unusually concrete Pentagon commitment. In May, the Defense Department announced that once Castelion completes testing and validation, it will award a two-year multi-year procurement contract for a minimum of 500 Blackbeard missiles per year, with options extending up to five years — and that it is seeking authorization and appropriations to buy more than 12,000 Blackbeard missiles over five years.

The Navy is moving in parallel. In April, Castelion received a $105 million Navy contract supporting Blackbeard's integration onto the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet, followed by a $23.4 million order covering 50 early-operational-capability pre-production missiles. A pair of Blackbeard missiles flew on a Super Hornet during a developmental test flight on Sept. 18, 2026. The weapon could eventually reach Navy ships and submarines as well.

The broader push reflects a shift toward lower-cost precision weapons that can be manufactured simply and at scale — increasingly with non-traditional contractors. Castelion, founded by former SpaceX engineers, says it has completed more than 20 developmental flights and is expanding its own production facilities to meet the expected demand.

aircraft-carriers-october-2026-bush-wash.content:
The USS George H.W. Bush pulled into Phuket, Thailand, on Oct. 4 for its first liberty call after 188 consecutive days at sea, leaving the USS George Washington as the Navy's only aircraft carrier supporting operations against Iran.

The visit, announced by U.S. 7th Fleet, marks the Bush's first port call since the carrier deployed from the continental United States on March 31. Guided-missile destroyer USS Delbert D. Black escorted the flattop from its previous station in the Arabian Sea. Reuters reported about 4,800 personnel were aboard for the rest-and-recreation break, with local media reporting the crew would be ashore from Oct. 4 to Oct. 9.

The Bush had been operating in U.S. Central Command's area of responsibility since April, when the United States briefly had three carriers on station in support of operations against Iran. "For the last six months, the strike group supported Operation Epic Fury and the U.S. naval blockade in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility to secure maritime security and stability in the Middle East," according to the 7th Fleet statement. The carrier reached the theater via the Cape of Good Hope, avoiding the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

The departure leaves a single carrier strike group — led by the Washington — in the Middle East for the first time in months. The Wall Street Journal and USNI News have reported that the USS Theodore Roosevelt will deploy to the Middle East, which could briefly restore a multi-carrier presence, though any overlap would be temporary under normal rotation schedules.

## Lincoln's marathon deployment

Across the Pacific, the USS Abraham Lincoln was holding off the coast of California to disembark Carrier Air Wing 9 and offload ammunition ahead of a homecoming this week, after the Washington relieved it in August. The Lincoln departed San Diego on Nov. 21, 2025; its return closes out a 321- to 322-day deployment — just short of the 326-day record the USS Gerald R. Ford set in May, and the second-longest deployment of the modern carrier era.

The marathon cruise drew scrutiny in August over grueling conditions aboard, including supply shortages and difficult living arrangements. Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao called media accounts dishonest while acknowledging adjustments to meal plans and limited calls home, and wrote in a letter to Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand — obtained by CNN — that at least eight personnel across the strike group attempted suicide during the deployment.

## A fleet stretched thin

The rest of the carrier fleet underscores the strain. The USS Ronald Reagan pulled into San Diego on Oct. 5 after departing Bremerton, Washington, on Sept. 30, following a 17-month drydocking availability during which she received an Unmanned Air Warfare Center to command and control the MQ-25 tanker drone — making her the second carrier with the upgrade, after the Theodore Roosevelt.

The USS Dwight D. Eisenhower returned to Naval Station Norfolk on Oct. 5 after an eight-day underway that ended with the loss of an EA-18G Growler on Sept. 28. The Navy attributed the mishap to a failure of the arresting gear; both crew members ejected safely and were rescued by helicopter, and the ship returned for a comprehensive assessment of its launch and recovery equipment.

And the USS Harry S. Truman moved into dry dock at Newport News Shipbuilding on Sept. 30 to begin her mid-life Refueling and Complex Overhaul. The Navy has eleven carriers on paper, but maintenance, refueling, and workups mean far fewer are deployable at any given time — a reality the 188-day Bush cruise and the 322-day Lincoln deployment make plain.

first-f16-block-72-flown-morocco.content:
The first F-16 Block 72 has taken to the air, seven years after Morocco became the launch customer for the newest variant of the Fighting Falcon.

Lockheed Martin announced Oct. 6 that the first jet built for the Royal Moroccan Air Force — a two-seat F-16D — completed its maiden flight at the company's facility in Greenville, South Carolina. The aircraft will now proceed through flight testing ahead of its delivery to Morocco. It is the first Block 72 airframe ever built, making Morocco the variant's launch operator.

Morocco was the first customer to select the Block 72 configuration when the U.S. government approved the proposed sale in March 2019. At the time, the Defense Security Cooperation Agency said Morocco was seeking 25 F-16C/D Block 72 aircraft in a package estimated at $3.787 billion, including 29 Pratt & Whitney F100-PW-229 engines — four of them spares — and 26 AN/APG-83 Scalable Agile Beam Radar (SABR) AESA radars, one of them a spare. The gap between that approval and the maiden flight runs to seven and a half years.

Photos of the flight showed the pilot wearing a Digital Joint Helmet Mounted Cueing System, an advanced helmet not often seen on F-16 pilots, though it is unclear whether Morocco has ordered it.

## A Block 70 with a Pratt & Whitney heart

The distinction between the Block 70 and the Block 72 is the engine. The Block 70 uses General Electric's F110-GE-129; the Block 72 uses Pratt & Whitney's F100-PW-229, which Lockheed Martin notes provides fractionally more power. The two configurations otherwise share the same major modernization package: the APG-83 AESA radar, new mission computers, Link 16 data links, modernized navigation, helmet-mounted cueing, and a structural life extended to 12,000 hours.

The F-16 began life as a Pratt & Whitney-powered fighter, and reliability problems with early F100s prompted the Air Force's "Alternate Fighter Engine" competition of the 1980s — the "Great Engine War" that established the F110 as an alternative. U.S. procurement eventually concentrated on GE-powered F-16s, but Pratt & Whitney continued supplying F100-powered jets to international customers.

For Morocco, the choice is about commonality. The Royal Moroccan Air Force already operates F-16C/D Block 52+ aircraft powered by F100 engines, so mechanics, spares, and engine shops carry over to the new fleet. Morocco is also upgrading its 23 remaining Block 52+ aircraft to the F-16V configuration — broadly similar to the new-build Block 70/72 standard — which would grow its F-16 fleet from 23 to 48 aircraft.

## Building an industrial base

Lockheed Martin is tying the program to a broader effort to develop Morocco's sustainment infrastructure. The company says it is working with Moroccan industry, including Maintenance Aero Maroc, on a maintenance, repair and overhaul facility at Benslimane spanning more than 8,000 square meters. Initially intended for heavy maintenance of C-130 Hercules aircraft, the facility is planned to expand to additional platforms including the F-16 — a step toward Morocco becoming a regional MRO hub.

Lockheed Martin's partnership with Morocco spans more than 50 years, beginning with the first C-130H delivery in 1974, the company said. Today the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces also operate Black Hawks and advanced radars, and are set to receive HIMARS and AH-64E Apache helicopters.

The new-build Moroccan jets arrive at an interesting point in the F-16 program. The Block 70/72 has attracted customers across Europe, the Middle East, and Asia — Bahrain, Bulgaria, Jordan, Slovakia, Taiwan, Turkey, and others have selected the latest-generation Viper — and the Greenville line now carries a backlog stretching years into the future. Morocco's position as the Block 72 launch customer means the jet now flying is effectively the prototype-standard production aircraft for a configuration other countries can now buy.

northrop-grumman-talon-blue-cca-flown.content:
Northrop Grumman's Talon Blue — now carrying the official designation YFQ-48A — has made its first flight, entering the Air Force's collaborative combat aircraft race as flying hardware rather than a viewgraph.

The company announced Oct. 3 that the uncrewed aircraft completed its first fully autonomous flight over the Mojave Air and Space Port in California, including taxi, takeoff, in-flight maneuvers, and landing. The aircraft was built by Scaled Composites, Northrop Grumman's subsidiary known for experimental designs, which developed it largely in secrecy before a formal unveiling at Mojave in December 2025. The Air Force assigned the YFQ-48A designation around the turn of the year — in the Pentagon's designation system, Y marks a prototype, F a fighter mission, and Q an unmanned aircraft.

Northrop developed Talon Blue entirely with company funds under its internally-funded Project Talon portfolio. The pitch centers on cost and production speed: the company says manufacturing and design innovations cut part count and overall weight, lowering cost and enabling faster production. The aircraft's high engine intake, wide-set landing gear, and integrated internal weapons bay are designed to support a range of missions for U.S. and allied customers. It is powered by a Pratt & Whitney PW500-series turbofan — an engine family better known from business jets — and flew under the civil registration N444LX, reaching about 233 knots and just over 10,000 feet on its first flight, according to flight-tracking data cited by Aviation Week.

Craig Woolston, Northrop's vice president and general manager for research and advanced design, said customers had made clear they need autonomous systems that can be fielded faster and more affordably without sacrificing mission effectiveness. "We listened," he said. "Talon Blue's first flight is one step toward a new generation of autonomous capabilities."

## Chasing Increment 2

Talon Blue enters a crowded field. The Air Force has moved its Increment 1 CCAs — Anduril's YFQ-44 and General Atomics' YFQ-42 — into production after deep flight testing, and the service plans to field at least 500 CCAs by 2032. Talon Blue is aimed at the follow-on Increment 2 acquisition, whose requirements have not yet been defined.

The competition includes Boeing's MQ-28 Ghost Bat, Lockheed Martin's tailless Vectis, and Kratos' FQ-58 Valkyrie, alongside offerings from new players and foreign manufacturers. For Northrop, a win matters beyond the drone program itself: with the F/A-XX next-generation naval fighter award going to Boeing, a CCA contract would bring the company back into the Pentagon's tactical air combat portfolio.

Northrop has also emphasized the autonomy ecosystem behind the aircraft, including its Model 437-based Talon IQ testbed — formerly known as Beacon — which matures autonomous mission software more cheaply than full-scale prototypes. The company cites seven decades of autonomy experience and more than 500,000 autonomous flight hours feeding into the program.

The broader bet is that advanced uncrewed tactical aircraft will be less risky and potentially more lucrative than traditional fighter programs, as air combat shifts toward predominantly uncrewed capabilities built in large numbers. Talon Blue's first autonomous flight is an early step — but in a race the Air Force is running at speed, flying hardware counts.

b1b-bombers-hasty-departure-england-iran.content:
U.S. Air Force B-1B Lancer bombers have made a hasty departure from RAF Fairford in England, pulling out of the forward base that hosted them during this year's combat operations against Iran after commanders received new intelligence about an Iran-backed threat to the installation.

All 12 of the B-1s stationed at the Gloucestershire airfield left over the weekend, local aircraft spotters and aviation photographers reported, with the jets departing in several waves on Sunday, Oct. 4. A U.S. defense official confirmed the withdrawal to The War Zone, and the Pentagon later acknowledged that every American bomber deployed to Fairford had re-deployed to home stations in the United States. It was the first time in months that the base hosted no U.S. bombers.

## A threat that escalated in hours

The withdrawal was highly unusual for an allied base in a peacetime country thousands of miles from a combat zone. The Times reported that some bombers and their crews departed while aerial refueling tankers were still being scrambled to support the transatlantic flight — a measure of how quickly the order came. At least three of the Lancers had already landed at their home base in South Dakota by Sunday.

According to the Times, commanders acted after receiving new threats about an Iran-backed plot against the installation — warnings that had been building for three weeks before urgency spiked in the previous 24 hours. The Pentagon would not confirm the nature of the intelligence, and the Wall Street Journal was the first to report the departure.

President Donald Trump confirmed on Monday that the threats drove the decision. "They didn't fly out by accident," he told reporters outside the White House. "There were some threats." He added that the United States knew the people behind them. Vice President JD Vance also confirmed the move and accused Iran of plotting attacks against the United States, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio pointed to the "hands of a foreign actor."

## A week of arrests near the base

The evacuation followed a string of arrests around Fairford. On Sept. 27, five men were detained near the base on suspicion of driving vans toward it. Gasoline was found in the vehicles but no explosives, and all five were released on bail. On Oct. 1, a 25-year-old British-Iranian dual national was arrested in London on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts and released on bail; days later, a 22-year-old was arrested in Westminster. No one has been charged.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were strong indications that Iran was behind the suspected plot. Iran denied the accusations, called them baseless, and summoned the British ambassador in Tehran over the matter.

The base was already under a spotlight. Iran had openly threatened Fairford in July, after the airfield's role in strikes on Iranian targets became clear. "Any base that is used to invade Iran's territory is our legitimate goal," Iran's Tasnim News Agency claimed on Telegram on July 23, referring to B-1s flying from Fairford.

## Fairford's role in the Iran campaign

Fairford has been a central hub of the U.S. bomber campaign against Iran. The base hosted a mix of B-1s and B-52s earlier this year, with the total bomber presence at the Gloucestershire hub peaking at 21 to 23 strategic bombers. Six B-52s returned across the Atlantic in a drawdown late last month, leaving about a dozen B-1s — some of which had arrived only days earlier as part of a normal force rotation — to be evacuated.

Stationing bombers at Fairford sharply reduced the flight time needed to reach targets in Iran. The Pentagon emphasized that the withdrawal does not affect readiness.

"The Airmen that operate America's bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities — including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States — anywhere, anytime," the Pentagon said. Both B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s have demonstrated those long-range strikes during this year's operations.

The bombers' repositioning may only be temporary. Fairford remains the U.S. military's forward bomber hub in the United Kingdom — and a fresh reminder that the facilities behind the Iran campaign are themselves in Tehran's sights.

coast-guard-mq9b-drones-248-million.content:
The U.S. Coast Guard has ordered its first MQ-9B drones, buying four of the long-range unmanned aircraft for $247.8 million in a move that gives the maritime service its own persistent airborne eyes for the first time.

The purchase, announced Oct. 9, covers four General Atomics aircraft along with ground control stations and supporting equipment, bought through a U.S. Customs and Border Protection contract. The aircraft are not expected to carry weapons, a service spokesperson told Breaking Defense. They will support offshore surveillance, search-and-rescue operations, and counter-narcotics missions — a broad charter for a service that patrols enormous areas with a relatively small fleet of cutters and aircraft.

## From borrowed drones to its own fleet

The Coast Guard is no stranger to the MQ-9, but until now it has always flown someone else's. The service has partnered with CBP since the mid-2000s to operate the border agency's MQ-9A drones, mostly out of Texas. According to a Coast Guard factsheet, those borrowed aircraft helped CBP seize 60,700 pounds of illegal drugs and catch roughly 20 smugglers in fiscal year 2026 alone.

Owning its own airframes changes the equation. "The MQ-9B long-range unmanned aircraft systems will expand our reach and strengthen our ability to protect the nation," said Anthony Antognoli, the assistant commandant and program executive officer for robotics and autonomous systems, in the Coast Guard's announcement. "This investment will give Coast Guard crews a longer-range view of our maritime domain, helping them detect threats earlier, make better-informed decisions and act faster across our missions."

The funding traces back to the FY25 reconciliation package — the "One Big Beautiful Bill" signed into law in July 2025 — which directed nearly $25 billion to the Coast Guard, along with FY26 appropriations. The service first revealed its MQ-9 plans last year, when Military Times reported that about $266 million of the reconciliation money was earmarked for the drones.

## What four drones buy

The MQ-9B is the long-range variant of the Reaper family, and its numbers explain the Coast Guard's interest. General Atomics says the SeaGuardian version is designed to conduct maritime intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions lasting more than 30 hours at a time, with a mission radius of roughly 1,200 nautical miles. For a service whose ships can take days to reach a distant smuggling corridor, that kind of persistence — a single aircraft watching an area for a day and a half, then handing off to a relief crew without missing a beat — is hard to get any other way.

That endurance compares favorably with what the Coast Guard flies today. A Coast Guard C-130 patrols for about 14 hours at a stretch, with a small crew working continuously throughout. With the MQ-9, crews rotate roughly every two hours, keeping a fresh set of eyes on the sensor feed while the aircraft stays on station.

The SeaGuardian variant is purpose-built for over-water work, with maritime radar, automatic identification system receivers, and the ability to dispense and monitor sonobuoys for anti-submarine missions. The Coast Guard did not say whether its aircraft will be the SeaGuardian version, and a service spokesperson did not answer that question, according to Defense Daily.

## A bigger aviation build-up

The drone buy is one piece of a much larger Coast Guard aviation recapitalization. FlightGlobal reported the service also ordered six new C-130J transports as part of a roughly $3 billion effort to modernize its air fleet, with the aircraft positioned as long-range maritime patrol platforms in their own right.

For a service long accustomed to making do with hand-me-downs and borrowed time on other agencies' drones, the MQ-9B order marks a step toward persistent, unmanned surveillance across America's maritime approaches. The drones will detect, classify, and track activity well before it reaches the homeland — giving cutters and boarding teams the one thing they can never get enough of: time.

lockheed-pac3-edge-next-gen-patriot.content:
Lockheed Martin has unveiled the PAC-3 Edge, its next-generation Patriot interceptor — and is backing the missile with hundreds of millions of dollars of its own money before the Army has even settled on the final requirement.

The missile, revealed Oct. 9 just ahead of the Association of the U.S. Army's annual conference, is Lockheed's bid for the Army's Future Interceptor program, which seeks a successor to the current PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE). Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed's missiles and fire control division, told Breaking Defense the company was one of two firms selected to advance in the program. He declined to name the other competitor, and the Army did not respond to a request for comment.

## What Edge changes

The PAC-3 is the Patriot system's hit-to-kill interceptor, designed to destroy incoming ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and aircraft by slamming into them directly rather than exploding nearby. It has seen real combat in the Middle East and Ukraine, where Patriot batteries have become some of the most valuable — and most heavily targeted — air defense assets in the world.

Edge promises to take that performance further. "PAC-3 Edge will be longer ranged. It'll be higher altitude. It'll be more capable to take on targets that are trying to hide," Cahill said. "It'll have greater sensitivity in its seeker. It'll have greater capability to maneuver and to respond to threats."

The missile pairs a new in-house seeker with a multi-pulse solid rocket motor developed with Northrop Grumman. The seeker was designed by Lockheed's Strigo Product Center, and the company says the motor's pulsed thrust gives the interceptor greater range and altitude throughout its flight than the legacy PAC-3. Control-system upgrades are aimed at delivering that performance against maneuvering targets, including the hypersonic weapons that are stressing current interceptors.

Lockheed plans to begin testing the missile in 2027, with a first deployment targeted for 2031. The company displayed a full-scale model of the weapon at AUSA.

## Lockheed's big bet

The scale of Lockheed's own investment is the real story. The company has already put between $50 million and $100 million into the missile itself, Cahill said — and it intends to spend hundreds of millions more. The seeker effort is bigger still: Lockheed plans to invest about $800 million in the seeker, having already spent "several" hundred million dollars on it, and intends to apply the technology across both offensive and defensive systems.

That confidence is not without a business case. Demand for air defense is at historic highs, driven by conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, and stockpiles are strained. In January, Lockheed signed a seven-year framework agreement with the Pentagon to expand PAC-3 manufacturing capacity from about 600 interceptors a year to 2,000. In July, the Army awarded the company a contract worth up to $58.6 billion to ramp up PAC-3 production, Reuters reported. Cahill told Reuters that the Edge would cost roughly the same as the current PAC-3 MSE, with an annual production rate of about 2,000 units at full production.

Edge would be built on Lockheed's existing PAC-3 line in Camden, Arkansas. The company is building a new MSE production facility there equipped with robotics and advanced manufacturing automation, with production set to move into the new plant — and the legacy facility to receive the same upgrades. "Before we ever get to the point where we're producing Edge, we will have already outfitted the entire factory from end to end with the most modern manufacturing capability available," Cahill said.

## A program that keeps coming back

The Future Interceptor program follows a fits-and-starts effort by the Army to develop a next-generation Patriot interceptor. In 2024, the service announced plans to cancel the Lower-Tier Future Interceptor (LTFI) program, which had seen Raytheon and Lockheed competing to build the new missile. A year later, an Army official suggested the program could move forward after all.

Earlier this year, Lockheed also announced the PAC-3 ACE, a less capable and lower-cost version of the MSE intended for international customers. Edge is the opposite play: the highest-performance interceptor Lockheed can build for the hardest targets the Army expects to face.

hanwha-army-tracked-howitzer-k9.content:
South Korea's Hanwha is not done winning American artillery contracts. Weeks after the Army tapped its wheeled K9 howitzer for a prototype program, the company says it will enter the service's new competition for a tracked variant — offering either its K9A1 or K9A2 self-propelled guns.

"I think it's a must. I mean, when we had early conversations with the Army, we actually thought the Army might be procuring tracked [variants] first," said Mike Smith, Hanwha USA's chief operating officer and president of Land Systems.

## A menu of tracked options

Hanwha USA is looking at a "menu of options" for the tracked competition, Smith said. The K9A1 is the widely fielded and most cost-effective choice, while the newer K9A2 brings more automation and firepower. According to Hanwha, the K9A1 mounts a 155mm, 52-caliber cannon with a range of over 40 kilometers, firing six to eight rounds per minute for three minutes at full capacity.

The K9A2 is the company's next step. It keeps the same drive power as the K9A1 but adds a fully automated turret capable of nine to ten rounds per minute, two independent loading arms for projectiles and propellants, and a new autoloader system that raises the rate of fire while cutting the crew size. Both are members of the K9 Thunder family, one of the most successful artillery systems in the world — in service with South Korea and exported to Poland, Norway, Finland, Australia, Romania, and others.

The Army laid the groundwork for the competition on Sept. 30, when its Program Acquisition Executive for Fires posted a request for information seeking tracked howitzers and a companion resupply vehicle. The solicitation asked vendors about production lead times, maximum production capacity, and strategies for moving production to the United States if their facilities are overseas. An industry day for interested vendors was scheduled for the following week.

Smith suggested Hanwha's existing production lines could shorten the wait: several K9 variants are already in service with land forces around the world. The howitzers are also "completely tailorable," he added — Hanwha can tweak its vehicles to meet the Army's formal requirements.

## The wheeled win that set the stage

Hanwha's bid for the tracked program follows its victory in the wheeled competition, where it beat an unusually crowded field. The Army awarded Hanwha Defense USA a deal worth up to $233 million for the accelerated delivery of six wheeled prototype howitzers, with an option for 12 more. Soldiers will use the prototypes — known as Mobile Tactical Cannon systems — in operational experiments to assess performance, reliability, and supportability in realistic combat conditions.

The losers were a who's-who of global artillery: an Elbit America team with Anduril and Oshkosh Defense offering the SIGMA platform, Leonardo DRS with KNDS and a Caesar-based gun, Germany's Rheinmetall with its Remote Controlled Howitzer 155, and Britain's BAE Systems with Archer.

Hanwha is already laying industrial groundwork in the United States. The company signed a three-year lease on an idle automobile plant in Opelika, Alabama, in April as an integration and test facility for the howitzer program, and Korean media estimate a future mass-production contract — planned for 2027, with initial fielding in 2030 — could reach about 500 guns worth roughly $7.1 billion.

## Why the Army wants both

An Army spokesperson told Breaking Defense the service is pursuing the two variants separately because they "address different operational requirements and formations." The wheeled howitzer is meant to give formations equipped with towed artillery more mobility, survivability, and responsiveness. The tracked variant is intended to keep up with armored formations. Both are aimed at replacing the towed M777 — some of which are 30 to 40 years old — and the self-propelled M109A7, a design first fielded in the 1960s.

The urgency comes from Ukraine, where massed tube artillery has remained decisive even in an age of drones and precision missiles. The Army wants guns that shoot farther, fire faster, and move before enemy counter-battery radar can answer — lessons written in Ukraine that Hanwha's K9, with its automation and rapid-fire rate, was built to deliver.

army-lasers-blast-drones-border-mhel.content:
An Army high-energy laser has shot down three hostile drones near the southern border over two nights in August, in one of the clearest real-world demonstrations yet that directed-energy weapons have moved from the laboratory to the fight.

Service members assigned to Joint Task Force Southern Border — a U.S. Northern Command unit that supports Customs and Border Protection — used the Army's Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser, known as AMP-HEL, to engage and defeat the three drones on Aug. 25 and 26. The aircraft were judged hostile based on their direct support of activity threatening U.S. military personnel and CBP partners, according to the Defense Department, and the footage of the engagements was later released by the Department of War.

## Cartels in the crosshairs

The drones were believed to be linked to Mexican drug cartels, which have made small unmanned aircraft a standard part of their smuggling operations. Cartel networks use cheap quadcopters to scout Border Patrol positions, monitor American personnel, and watch for gaps in border defenses — all without putting an operative physically across the border.

"Cartel networks are increasingly employing unmanned aircraft systems to facilitate illicit human-smuggling and actively spy on our personnel and law enforcement partners," said Army Maj. Gen. Curtis Taylor, commander of Joint Task Force Southern Border. "By integrating layered countermeasures alongside advanced directed-energy capabilities like this laser system, we have made it clear that we will not tolerate hostile surveillance."

The AMP-HEL system was built with directed-energy technology from AeroVironment, and its deployment to the border marks a significant operational milestone. High-energy lasers have been "five years away" for decades, dogged by problems with power, cooling, and keeping a beam steady on a moving target long enough to burn through it. The August engagements suggest those problems are now being solved in the field.

## A surge of incursions

The laser shots came against a backdrop of escalating drone activity. The military detected 378 drone incursions along the southern border in the previous 30 days alone, Brig. Gen. Brian Filler, the task force's deputy commander for operations, told reporters — and the trend is increasing. Most of the aircraft are commercial off-the-shelf models carrying surveillance cameras, often observed flying alongside cross-border smuggling movements.

And the August engagement was not an isolated event. The U.S. military said earlier in October it had downed 11 cartel drones with high-energy lasers since deploying the technology to the border region in August.

The Army has responded by making the desert a proving ground. At Falcon Peak, a Northern Command exercise held in September at Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona, soldiers watched as defense firms demonstrated radars, interceptor drones, autonomous gun systems, and directed-energy weapons designed to detect, track, and destroy small unmanned aircraft. The exercise established permanent counter-drone testing lanes at Yuma — a sign the Army expects the small-drone threat to keep growing.

## Lasers change the cost math

What makes the laser engagements striking is the economics. A cartel drone costs a few hundred or a few thousand dollars. Shooting one down with a missile interceptor costing hundreds of thousands of dollars is a losing trade; dropping one with a beam that costs roughly the price of the fuel running its generator is not. A laser weapon can engage targets repeatedly, at the speed of light, for as long as it has power and a clear line of sight.

That cost exchange is also the military's answer to a lesson from Ukraine, where cheap drones have transformed the battlefield and driven rapid, field-level innovation in both attack and defense. Army planners say they want to reproduce that rapid innovation cycle at home — and the border, with its daily stream of hostile drones, has become their laboratory.

The Army has not said whether the laser will be deployed to the border permanently. But with 11 confirmed kills and hundreds of incursions a month, the case for keeping it there is writing itself.

texas-guard-ah64e-apaches-jbsa-lackland.content:
The first three AH-64E Apache attack helicopters assigned to the Texas Army National Guard's 1st Battalion, 149th Aviation Regiment touched down at Kelly Field, Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, on Sept. 24, 2026, opening a months-long relocation that folds the Guard battalion into one of the Army's most contested force-structure overhauls in decades.

The move places the 1-149th — a National Guard reconnaissance battalion under the 36th Combat Aviation Brigade, 36th Infantry Division — at Kelly Field as part of what the Army calls its reformatting plan, the service's broad effort to reshape aviation around fewer, more modern aircraft.

For the battalion, the relocation is the second phase of a transformation that began in February. On Feb. 3, 2026, the 1st Battalion, 101st Aviation Regiment — the active-duty "No Mercy" battalion at Fort Campbell, Kentucky — transferred its first two AH-64E Apache Version 4 helicopters to the Texas and Mississippi Guards, with the 1-149th receiving the airframes as the 101st made room for the incoming Version 6 upgrade.

Lt. Col. Cody Anfinson, the 1-149th's commander, described the handover as a milestone for a unit with long Apache roots. The battalion retired the last AH-64A in the entire Army back in July 2012 — tail number 90-00451, flown out of Ellington Field in Houston — and has waited more than a decade to step into the Army's latest attack helicopter.

## A Guard battalion at the center of Army reform

The relocation lands the 1-149th squarely in the middle of the Army Transformation Initiative, launched by a Pentagon memo in April 2025 and now being executed across the aviation branch. Under the plan, the active-duty AH-64E fleet is shrinking from 408 airframes to 240, with the newest helicopters transferring into the National Guard. Eleven active air cavalry squadrons and two reserve expeditionary combat aviation brigades are being disbanded, older AH-64D models are being decommissioned outright, and roughly 6,500 aviation positions are being cut across 2026 and 2027, according to figures reported by Aviation Week and cited by Defense Express.

Army leaders have framed the cuts as a trade: fewer helicopters, but newer ones, concentrated where they can be sustained. The Guard, with its deep maintenance experience, is being positioned as the long-term home for the Apache even as the active force pivots toward unmanned systems and next-generation aircraft.

The 1-149th's structure reflects the Guard model. Its headquarters sits at Ellington Field Joint Reserve Base in Houston; Company A belongs to the Mississippi Army National Guard, while Companies B and C are Texas units. Consolidating the battalion at Kelly Field brings its aircraft, maintainers, and crews under one roof at an installation with deep aviation roots — Kelly Field has launched military aircraft for more than a century.

## Version 4 today, Version 6 tomorrow

The helicopters arriving in San Antonio are AH-64E Version 4 aircraft, the configuration the 101st is shedding as it converts to Version 6 — a standard that brings improved rotor blades, larger fuel capacity, and a large-area cockpit display, according to Boeing. For a Guard battalion that flew the oldest Apaches in the Army just over a decade ago, the Version 4 aircraft represent a generational jump in sensors, networking, and lethality.

The relocation is expected to take months to complete as aircraft, equipment, and personnel flow south from the battalion's current stations. When finished, the 1-149th will be one of the Guard's most modern attack battalions — and a test case for the Army's bet that the National Guard can carry a larger share of the service's attack aviation future.

osprey-mv22b-sonobuoy-asw-test.content:
An MV-22B Osprey dropped sonobuoys over the Pacific off San Clemente Island, California, on Aug. 19, 2026, completing the first lot acceptance test of the sensors from a tiltrotor — a milestone the Navy says could reshape how it keeps its undersea surveillance inventory honest.

The test brought together the Air Anti-Submarine Warfare Systems Program Office (PMA-264), the V-22 Joint Program Office (PMA-275), and Marine Operational Test and Evaluation Squadron 1 (VMX-1), flying an aircraft out of Marine Corps Air Station Miramar. It was announced Sept. 22 by PMA-264 and detailed in a Defense Department release the following day.

The mission was not a combat exercise. It was an acceptance run for the Navy's Sonobuoy Quality Assurance Program, which pulls random production samples of sonobuoys and drops them over water to verify reliability and acoustic performance before the lots reach operational squadrons. Until now, that job belonged to the P-3C Orions of Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 30 (VX-30), using automated cockpit-triggered launchers.

## Manual drops from the ramp

The Osprey did it the hard way. With the rear cargo ramp open, crew chiefs manually removed the buoys' container caps and inverted the launch tubes into the slipstream — a hands-on evolution a world away from the P-3's push-button dispensers. Defense Department photographs show the loading and rigging work at Miramar in the days before the flight.

Navy Capt. Greg Hinkle, PMA-264's program manager, said the focus of the quality assurance program is making sure the sonobuoys delivered to the fleet perform exactly as expected, and that using the Osprey for the mission reinforces the supply chain and ensures front-line aircrews have mission-ready stores to detect and track undersea threats.

The test gives the Navy a dependable substitute if its primary test platforms are unavailable, preventing backlogs in the acceptance pipeline as the P-3C fleet winds down.


The test crew came from VMX-1, the Marine Corps' operational test squadron at Miramar — the same community that wrings out every new Marine aircraft before it reaches the fleet. Their involvement signals that the Navy views the Osprey not as a one-off test mule but as a standing member of the sonobuoy enterprise.

There is precedent. A 2025 photograph from the Philippine Sea showed a VMM-265 crew chief handling sonobuoys aboard an Osprey with the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit — evidence that the fleet has been quietly working the problem for at least a year. The August test formalized it: the tiltrotor is now a validated, dependable substitute in the quality-assurance chain, the backstop that keeps acceptance testing moving when the P-3Cs are down or tasked elsewhere.

## A door left open

The official release frames the event as laying the groundwork for expanded tactical employment across the fleet — careful language that stops short of declaring the Osprey an operational submarine hunter. But the implications are hard to miss. A tiltrotor that can sprint to a datum far faster than a helicopter and then slow to work a contact has obvious appeal for anti-submarine warfare, and Marine crews have been experimenting at the margins for years: a 2025 photograph showed a VMM-265 crew chief handling sonobuoys in the Philippine Sea.

For now, the verified achievement is narrower and arguably more important: the supply chain that feeds the fleet's ears in the water has a new, faster backup. In a Pacific where submarines are the pacing threat, that is not a small thing.

sea-drone-rescued-apache-crew-saronic.content:
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth stood on the factory floor of Saronic Technologies in Austin, Texas, on Sept. 18, 2026, and called the startup "the gold standard" of American military manufacturing. He had a story to tell about why.

Three months earlier, on June 8, a U.S. Army AH-64 Apache patrolling over the Strait of Hormuz went down off the coast of Oman after taking Iranian fire — President Donald Trump later confirmed that Iran had shot the helicopter down. The two crew members ended up in the water, roughly two hours from help, in airspace too dangerous for a manned rescue helicopter.

The Navy sent a boat with no crew at all.

The vessel was a Corsair, a 24-foot autonomous surface vessel built by Saronic and operated by the 5th Fleet's Task Force 59, the Navy's unmanned-systems experimentation unit. It reached the downed aviators, who hauled themselves aboard, then moved them to a second location because of what U.S. Central Command described as operational circumstances. From there a helicopter hoisted them out. Both crew members were reported stable.

Defense officials believe it was the first known personnel recovery ever carried out by an unmanned surface vessel.

## The "Arsenal of Freedom" tour

Hegseth's Austin stop was part of a swing he branded the "Arsenal of Freedom" tour, aimed at showcasing the commercial shipyards and startups the Pentagon wants to pull into its industrial base. Saronic's chief executive, Dino Mavrookas, introduced him, and the secretary used the visit to promise fast contracts for companies that deliver — and the door for those that don't.

The Corsair that made the pickup is no prototype. The 24-foot boat tops 35 knots, ranges 1,000 nautical miles, and carries a 1,000-pound payload. Saronic says it went from prototype to serial production of 300 hulls in under a year, backed by a $392 million late-2025 production contract and a $1.75 billion funding round in March 2026. The company is also building "Port Alpha," a $3.2 billion shipyard in South Texas whose first phase is expected to be operational by 2028.

## Why a robot boat

The rescue's backstory explains the decision. The Apache was one of at least seven crewed U.S. aircraft lost to Iranian fire since February 2026, during the U.S.-Iran conflict that began with Operation Epic Fury. Sending a manned helicopter into the same airspace to hover over survivors was judged too risky; the unmanned boat could go where crews could not.

CENTCOM said the operation was run by Naval Forces Central Command with the 82nd Airborne Division, and spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins confirmed the Corsair's role to DefenseScoop. Saronic co-founder Rob Lehman later walked through the mission on a DefenseScoop podcast, describing a vessel designed for exactly this kind of dull, dangerous work.

The Pentagon has not said whether the Corsair's rescue will become doctrine. But on a factory floor in Austin, the secretary of war treated it as a preview — of a fleet where the first responder to a downed crew might not have a crew at all.

us-panama-k1000-drones-6-million.content:
The United States handed Panama four long-range K1000 surveillance drones on Sept. 16, 2026, a package worth more than $6 million aimed at pushing the fight against drug trafficking and human smuggling farther from American shores.

U.S. Ambassador Kevin Marino Cabrera delivered the aircraft to Panama's Ministry of Public Security at a ceremony at Lieutenant Octavio Rodríguez Garrido Air Base in Panama Pacifico, with Panamanian Security Minister Frank Ábrego in attendance. The package was funded by U.S. Southern Command.

The drones will be flown by Panama's National Aeronaval Service, known as Senan, to monitor remote borders and safeguard strategic maritime corridors, according to the U.S. Embassy in Panama. The stated mission set: dismantling drug trafficking and human smuggling networks, and halting transnational threats long before they approach American soil — the embassy's own headline framed the delivery as protecting the American homeland.

## Pilots trained, then handed the keys

The handover doubled as a graduation. Ten newly certified Panamanian drone pilots received their qualifications the same day, completing a six-week, U.S.-funded training program led by Kraus Hamdani Aerospace, the American company that builds the K1000.

Cabrera tied the delivery to the administration's broader push, saying that under President Trump's leadership the United States is driving expanded security cooperation with Panama through concrete, results-oriented investments, and that scaling up joint capabilities on land and at sea is aimed at aggressively stopping transnational threats at the source.


The ceremony itself drew local attention. Abrego left a National Assembly budget session early to attend, a move that drew questions from opposition deputy Jonathan Vega, according to Panamanian outlet conven.org — a reminder that American security assistance, however welcome, is never politically free.

Senan, the recipient service, is Panama's combined air-and-sea arm, responsible for patrolling the country's long Pacific and Caribbean coastlines and the remote jungle border regions where smugglers move drugs north and migrants south. Persistent aerial surveillance has been the missing piece: Panama's forces have long relied on tip-offs and patrol craft, arriving after the fact. A drone that can watch a coastline for a full day changes that equation.

## A 45-pound workhorse

The K1000 is built for endurance rather than firepower. The 45-pound aircraft spans 16.4 feet, cruises up to 75 mph, and can stay aloft 24 hours in its solar-recharge configuration — 12 hours in vertical-takeoff mode — with a range of about 1,000 miles. It operates line-of-sight within 90 miles or beyond line-of-sight via satellite, and a three-person crew can unpack it from Pelican cases and have it flying in under 15 minutes.

That combination — long legs, tiny logistics footprint, no runway — is what makes it suited to Panama's geography: dense jungle borders, long coastlines, and the maritime corridors threading toward the canal.

The delivery landed amid a wider Pentagon shift. CNN has reported the Defense Department moving MQ-9 Reaper drones from Africa to Southern Command's area of responsibility, alongside months of U.S. strikes on alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. The K1000s give Panama its own persistent eye in the sky — American-funded, American-trained, but Panamanian-flown.

uss-george-washington-200000th-aircraft.content:
An F-35C Lightning II caught the number three wire aboard USS George Washington on Aug. 18, 2026, and made history doing it: the 200,000th fixed-wing aircraft recovery in the carrier's 34 years at sea.

The milestone trap happened as the ship steamed in the Indian Ocean. The pilot was Lt. Steven Frazier of Strike Fighter Squadron 147, the "Argonauts," flying a routine sortie in the U.S. 7th Fleet area of operations.

Rear Adm. Jeffrey L. Heames, commander of Carrier Strike Group 5, called the number a testament to the enduring strength of American naval aviation and the professionalism of the sailors who make it possible, adding that U.S. carriers remain ready to launch and recover aircraft anywhere, anytime.

## Thirty-four years of traps

George Washington was commissioned on July 4, 1992 — the sixth Nimitz-class carrier — and has been the Navy's only permanently forward-deployed carrier, homeported in Japan, since 2008. The aircraft it has recovered trace the evolution of naval aviation itself: F-14 Tomcats in the 1990s, legacy F/A-18 Hornets, then Super Hornets, EA-18G Growlers, E-2 Hawkeyes, and now the F-35C.

A trap is a violent, precise event. The aircraft snags a steel arresting cable with its tailhook at more than 140 miles per hour; a carrier at full tempo can land one aircraft per minute, roughly 70 a day. Two hundred thousand of them represents decades of flight-deck crews working in one of the most dangerous industrial environments on earth.

"For the George Washington, more than anything, it shows consistency over the last 34 years to be able to complete whatever mission the country calls upon it to do," Frazier said. "For me personally, it shows that if this aircraft carrier launches me off of the ship, I'll be able to come back and land on it."

The milestone also quietly underlines the durability of the Nimitz design. While the newer Ford class has wrestled with its launch and recovery systems, George Washington's counter kept turning — 200,000 recoveries without fanfare, on a hull commissioned when the Soviet Union had been gone barely seven months.


George Washington is the flagship of Carrier Strike Group 5, the Navy's only permanently forward-deployed strike group, homeported at Yokosuka, Japan. The 200,000th trap is as much a tribute to the ship's company — the catapult and arresting-gear crews, the ordnancemen, the controllers in the tower — as to the pilots. A carrier's trap count is the one statistic that cannot be spun: every number on that board was a real airplane, a real deck, a real wire.

## Straight into the fight

The celebration was brief. The ship's 7th Fleet patrol had already kept it at sea for months; the Arabian Sea tasking extended that deployment into one of the longest continuous forward operations of the carrier's career.

Two days after the milestone, George Washington sailed into the Arabian Sea to take over the Middle East mission from USS Abraham Lincoln, whose marathon deployment — including combat operations against Iran — was ending. The move left a temporary carrier gap in the Western Pacific, a trade the Navy accepted to keep pressure on in the Central Command theater.

aim260-jatm-australian-super-hornet.content:
A U.S. Navy photograph released Sept. 30, 2026, shows something airpower watchers have waited years to see clearly: an inert AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile riding the cheek station of an Australian F/A-18F Super Hornet.

The image, taken Sept. 11 by Navy photographer Dana Rene White, captures the Royal Australian Air Force jet — assigned to No. 1 Squadron — taking off from Naval Base Ventura County Point Mugu in California during Gray Flag 2026, the Navy's sprawling test exercise. The missile's blue bands mark it as an inert round: no live rocket motor, no warhead.

The loadout tells its own story. Alongside the AIM-260, the jet carried inert CATM-9X and CATM-120 training rounds, three external fuel tanks, an AN/ASQ-228 ATFLIR targeting pod, and a Tactical Combat Training System pod — a test configuration, not a war load.

## Australia's $480 million bet

The sighting came weeks after Australia announced in August 2026 that it would buy the AIM-260 through U.S. Foreign Military Sales, becoming the first country outside the United States to operate the missile. The deal is valued at roughly $480 million — reported in Australia as almost 736 million Australian dollars — with RAAF Super Hornets first in line, followed by the F-35A and the EA-18G Growler. The MQ-28 Ghost Bat has been named as a possible future candidate.

Canberra's own language was measured: the acquisition, Australia said, will give its air force a credible deterrent against airborne targets, complementing existing air-to-air missile capabilities. No delivery timeline has been disclosed.

## The missile meant to outrange the threat

The AIM-260, built by Lockheed Martin under a program the Pentagon launched in 2017, is designed to outrange the AIM-120 AMRAAM it will eventually succeed — prior reporting puts its reach at 120 miles or more — while keeping a similar form factor so it fits the internal weapons bays of the F-22 and F-35. Its development has been paced by China's PL-15, the very-long-range missile carried by the J-20.

The program is accelerating. In September 2026 the Pentagon and Lockheed Martin signed a framework agreement to push production and multiyear procurement, and the Air Force Test Center has confirmed both ground and airborne testing. The first-ever public photo of a U.S. AIM-260 appeared only in May 2026, on a VX-31 test jet at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida — making the Australian sighting the second public glimpse, and the first involving a foreign operator.

Gray Flag itself was the largest to date: more than 3,000 personnel, 150 organizations, 750 sorties, and 2,000 flight hours flown from the Point Mugu Sea Range.


The missile sighting is part of a wider U.S.-Australian air-weapons partnership. RAAF Super Hornets are also involved in the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile effort under the Southern Cross Integrated Flight Research Experiment, or SCIFiRE — a separate program, but evidence of how deeply the two air forces have intertwined their long-range strike planning.

One caution from the analysts who first published the photo: it does not establish whether the missile was Australian-owned, a U.S. test asset, or part of a specific integration effort. What it does establish is that the West's next long-range air-to-air missile is now flying on allied jets — inert for now, in public for the first time.

ukraine-f16-fleet-readiness-crisis.content:
More than half of Ukraine's donated F-16 fighters are stuck in what a Western official calls "maintenance limbo," and at the current pace Kyiv could exhaust its remaining available aircraft by the end of 2026, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sept. 30, 2026.

The Ukrainian Air Force declined to give the Journal fleet-status figures, so the assessment rests on Western sources — but Reuters independently confirmed the core of it on Oct. 8, reporting that many of the donated jets are back in western Europe for repairs, grounded by a lack of engine parts.

## The maintenance bottleneck

Ukraine has received an estimated 40 to 50 F-16s, with some airframes held back in Europe for training and five confirmed lost in combat. Another 110 have been pledged by Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, and Norway. The problem is not just airframes — it is the pipeline that keeps them flying.

Long-term maintenance is done in Belgium by Sabena Aerospace Engineering, where phase inspections are taking up to 40 weeks — against two to six weeks in the United States. For a fleet flying daily combat air-defense sorties, that math is brutal.

The timing could hardly be worse. Ukraine's F-16s have become workhorses of the air-defense campaign, thrown against Russian cruise missiles and, increasingly, Russia's new jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones. Analyst Michael Kofman has noted the Vipers playing an important role in those intercepts — the kind of grinding, unglamorous work that eats airframes.

## Running low on missiles

The jets are also running out of things to shoot. AIM-9 Sidewinders and AIM-120 AMRAAMs have been expended in large numbers against incoming missiles and drones, and the same AMRAAMs feed Ukraine's NASAMS ground-based air-defense batteries — two hungers drawing from one stockpile.

Ukrainian pilots are rationing missile shots and falling back on the F-16's internal 20mm M61A1 Vulcan cannon, with Kyiv negotiating for tens of thousands of additional 20mm rounds. It is a measure of the strain: a fourth-generation fighter reduced to gun runs because the missile pipeline cannot keep up.


The sustainment problem starts long before the flight line. Ukrainian pilots and maintainers trained in the United States, Denmark, and Romania on compressed timelines, and the maintenance culture they entered is unforgiving: an F-16 is a maintenance-hungry aircraft even in peacetime, a demand that only grows under combat tempo and dispersed basing. Spare engines, avionics boxes, and structural parts were always the long poles of the fleet — and they are now the poles that are breaking.

## A fleet pressed into a different war

The donated Vipers are older European mid-life-update airframes, pledged for air combat and strike missions. Instead they have been pressed into the air-defense grind — a role that burns through engines, parts, and missiles at a rate no peacetime sustainment plan contemplated.

Reuters framed the wider picture bluntly: Ukraine has, in essence, run out of the air-defense missiles that matter most. The F-16 fleet's troubles are one front in a broader air-defense crisis — one that Western capitals, well into the war's fourth year, have not solved. With winter approaching and Russia's drone and missile campaign showing no sign of easing, the pressure on the remaining flyable jets will only grow.

vfa41-epic-fury-weapons-expended.content:
A single Navy fighter squadron fired 421 missiles and bombs during Operation Epic Fury — and someone kept count.

A photograph of VFA-41's expenditure board, shared by aviation photographer Jeff Rojas, lays out the "Black Aces'" full wartime bill from the U.S. air campaign against Iran: 173 GBU-38 500-pound JDAMs, 52 GBU-31(V)4 bunker-buster 2,000-pounders, 48 dual-mode laser JDAMs, 41 JSOW glide bombs, 33 AIM-9X Sidewinders, 30 standard 2,000-pound JDAMs, 27 1,000-pound JDAMs, 10 SLAM-ER cruise missiles, 6 AIM-120 AMRAAMs, and a single GBU-12 laser-guided bomb.

The War Zone, which first published the tally, estimates the ordnance cost at roughly $43.6 million at minimum — derived from U.S. military budget documents, with the caveat that munitions pricing fluctuates and JDAM kit costs are hard to separate from the warheads they guide.

## Two months of war

VFA-41 flies the F/A-18F Super Hornet as part of the air wing aboard USS Abraham Lincoln. The Pentagon says Operation Epic Fury ran from Feb. 28 to May 5, 2026 — about nine weeks — though American strikes on Iranian targets continued intermittently afterward. Lincoln, on a marathon deployment stretching back to 2025, had just left the Middle East when the tally surfaced in early October, bound for home in San Diego.

The air-to-air portion of the list is its own story. Thirty-three AIM-9Xs and six AMRAAMs with no known kills of crewed Iranian aircraft — the missiles were almost certainly fired at Iranian drones, and possibly cruise missiles. After a crash program in 2024, Super Hornets can now carry up to nine air-to-air missiles per sortie, a configuration crews call the "Murder Hornet" loadout, built specifically for the drone threat.


The expenditure has reignited Washington's munitions debate. Precision weapons take years to build and cannot be surged overnight; Pentagon planners have warned for years that a high-end fight would burn through stockpiles faster than industry can replace them. Epic Fury — nine weeks, one squadron, 421 weapons — is now the freshest data point in that argument. Multiply the Black Aces' bill across Lincoln's four strike squadrons, the rest of the joint force, and the months of intermittent strikes that followed, and the industrial question answers itself.

## Markings of a drone war

The squadron's jets came home decorated. One VFA-41 Super Hornet, Bureau Number 168491, returned to Naval Air Station Lemoore on Oct. 1 with a broken-submarine silhouette painted under the cockpit labeled "Sub Buster" — believed to mark a kill on an Iranian submarine, a first for the type. Iranian Kilo-class and Ghadir midget submarines were priority targets throughout the campaign, and the Pentagon has previously confirmed submarine kills by other means, including an MQ-9's Hellfire and an Army ATACMS strike.

The Black Aces were not alone. A VMFA-314 F-35C "Black Knights" jet returned with its own battle markings: an oil tanker, three submarines, a surface combatant, a Shahed-type drone, artillery, and launcher silhouettes, with tally marks beside AIM-120, AGM-154, GBU-31, GBU-54, and GBU-32 silhouettes.

For scale: the entire Eisenhower strike group fired 770 munitions across eight months of Red Sea fighting in 2023-2024. One squadron fired 421 in about two. The Pentagon has released relatively little official data on Epic Fury's ordnance expenditure — which is precisely why a squadron scoreboard photographed by a civilian spotter became news. It is worth stating plainly: the 421 figure comes from that photograph, not from a Navy release.

germany-f125-frigates-iris-t-missiles.content:
Germany is finally giving its biggest warships real air defenses. On Oct. 2, 2026, Diehl Defence and the federal procurement office BAAINBw signed an adaptation development contract to fit the naval version of the IRIS-T SLM surface-to-air missile to the German Navy's four F125 frigates — nine days after the Bundestag's budget committee approved the program on Sept. 23.

Each 7,200-ton frigate will receive two deck-mounted launchers holding 16 missiles apiece: 32 interceptors per ship, in vertical-launch canisters, against aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and drones. The missile reaches 40 kilometers out and 20 kilometers up, guided by datalink with terminal self-homing.

The four ships of the Baden-Württemberg class — Baden-Württemberg, Nordrhein-Westfalen, Sachsen-Anhalt, Rheinland-Pfalz — were built for stabilization and crisis-management missions, and their armament showed it: short-range anti-ship missiles and two RIM-116 RAM point-defense launchers on a hull the size of a destroyer. The gap became a public embarrassment in 2024, when Baden-Württemberg detoured around Africa rather than transit the Red Sea on its return from an Indo-Pacific deployment.

## From concept to firing in ten months

The program is moving fast because the hard part is already done. In October 2025, during a naval firing exercise off Norway, engineers bolted a demonstrator launcher to the C-deck of Baden-Württemberg and engaged multiple targets using the ship's own radar data — going from concept to live firing in under ten months.

The naval adaptation strips out the ground system's support legs and hydraulics to save weight and deck space. Functional prototypes are expected in 2027, with sea trials and the first operational test launches the same year.


Diehl's own description of the goal is deliberately modest: "The aim is to make the system mission-capable on the German Navy's F125 frigates." But the engineering is not trivial. The naval IRIS-T SLM drops the ground launcher's support legs and hydraulics, fires from a compact vertical canister, and stays in contact with the ship via datalink until its own seeker takes over for the terminal phase — a fire-and-update architecture built for saturation attacks by drones and sea-skimmers.

## A missile with a combat record

The IRIS-T SLM is not a paper missile. German-supplied batteries in Ukraine have intercepted Shahed drones and Kh-101 and Kalibr cruise missiles at ranges up to 40 kilometers, and Berlin has explicitly cited that operational record in justifying the frigate upgrade.

The move fits Germany's broader post-2022 naval rearmament — new F126 frigates and Type 212CD submarines with Norway are in the pipeline alongside missile upgrades across the fleet. But the F125 fix is the most symbolically loaded: the ships were designed in an era when Berlin assumed its navy would police crises, not fight wars.

For a navy that watched its F124 frigate Hessen swat Houthi drones over the Red Sea under the EU's Operation Aspides while its newest, largest frigates lacked comparable defenses, the contract closes what The War Zone called one of the most conspicuous weaknesses in a Western fleet. Thirty-two missiles per ship will not make the F125 an air-defense destroyer. But it will, at last, give it teeth.

red-tails-f35-tuskegee-thunder-training.content:
For three days in mid-August, Dannelly Field in Montgomery, Alabama, became a war zone — simulated, but only just.

Operation Tuskegee Thunder, held Aug. 12-14, 2026, put the Alabama Air National Guard's 187th Fighter Wing through its paces in a scenario built around a Pacific operating environment. Airmen generated F-35A combat sorties while absorbing simulated attacks, degraded communications, chemical threats, drone incursions, casualties, gate runners, and mass-casualty drills — falling back on alternate and contingency command-and-control methods when their primary networks went down.

The exercise ran in conjunction with the wing's Combat Readiness Inspection, the formal evaluation of whether the Red Tails can generate and sustain combat airpower as part of the total force. For a wing that received its first F-35As in December 2023, transitioning from the F-16, it was the most important milestone of the conversion to date.

## "The entire wing has to be part of the fight"

"The F-35 is the most capable fighter aircraft in the world, but readiness is ultimately measured by our airmen's ability to fight and sustain operations in the most challenging conditions," said Col. John D. Caldwell, the wing's commander. "Operation Tuskegee Thunder provided our airmen the opportunity to hone their skills, refine tactics, techniques and procedures, and develop the confidence to operate anywhere, at any time."

Lt. Col. Martin "Lefty" Smith, an F-35 pilot who leads the wing's plans and programs, put the challenge in practical terms: operating a fifth-generation fighter in a contested environment requires the entire wing to be part of the fight — maintaining command and control, protecting and sustaining the force, adapting when the environment changes, and continuing to generate combat airpower. The challenge, he said, isn't simply launching aircraft.

## The inspection that matters

A Combat Readiness Inspection is the Air Force's periodic deep audit of a wing's ability to do its wartime job — not just fly, but deploy, communicate, protect, and sustain under pressure. For the 187th, passing through it with the F-35 validates years of conversion work: large-force exercises, night operations, and distributed training since the first Lightnings arrived at Dannelly Field.

The August inspection tested whether all of it holds together when the radios go down and the casualties start coming in — the unglamorous half of airpower, and the half that decides wars. The official releases describe what was tested, not how the wing scored; no outcome has been published.


The wing's path to the Lightning was a long one. The 187th flew the F-16 for decades before the first F-35As touched down at Dannelly Field in December 2023. Since then the conversion has run through the standard syllabus of a fighter wing changing airframes: large-force exercises to learn to fight as a package, night operations, and distributed training away from home station. Tuskegee Thunder was the exam that asked whether the wing could do all of it while someone was shooting back — at least on paper.

## A name with history

The Red Tails name honors the Tuskegee Airmen of World War II, the Black fighter pilots whose escort missions over Europe became legend. The 187th has carried that lineage through the F-16 era and into the F-35, and the exercise's name was no accident: Tuskegee Thunder was as much about heritage as readiness.
